title: Hurst v. W.J. Lake & Co.
summary: A trade practice for rounding protein measurements could explain a contract requiring at least 50 percent protein, despite the apparent precision of the written number.
notes: The surrounding notes distinguish usage of trade from a course of dealing between particular parties. They also examine whether a newcomer must know a usage before it can affect the contract.

sections.Parties: Hurst sold horse-meat scraps to W.J. Lake & Co. The seller sought the $700 that the buyer had deducted from payment under a protein-content adjustment clause.
sections.Material Facts:
The contract called for 350 tons of horse-meat scraps at $50 per ton, with a minimum protein content of 50 percent. It authorized a $5-per-ton reduction for material below that threshold. Testing showed that 140 tons contained between 49.53 and 49.96 percent protein, and the buyer paid $45 per ton for those shipments.

The seller alleged a usage in the parties’ trade under which a measurement of at least 49.5 percent counted as 50 percent for this purpose. Both parties were alleged to be members of the trade and to know the usage. The dispute therefore concerned how traders used the numerical specification, rather than whether the seller could erase a clear specification merely because compliance was inconvenient.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court resolved the matter against the seller on the pleadings. The Oregon Supreme Court reversed so that the alleged usage could be considered. The appellate decision did not itself find that the usage existed or finally award the disputed balance.
sections.Issue: Could the seller use evidence of a known trade practice to explain what the parties meant by “minimum 50 percent,” or would that evidence impermissibly contradict an unambiguous written term?
sections.Holding: The alleged usage was admissible to explain the agreement. Numerical language, like other contractual language, can have an established trade meaning that differs from an outsider’s literal reading.
sections.Reasoning:
The court rejected the premise that apparently precise words necessarily have a meaning independent of the setting in which the parties used them. Commercial communities may use familiar words, quantities, and measurements in specialized ways. If both parties contracted against that shared usage, applying it gives effect to their agreement.

The procedural posture matters. The seller was entitled to establish the practice it alleged; the decision did not dispense with the need to prove a practice sufficiently connected to the parties and their transaction. It therefore differs from an instruction to apply any asserted custom or to ignore express language whenever industry evidence is offered. The case also illustrates why the interpreter must distinguish an actual contradiction from an explanation of the sense in which the parties used the words.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Hurst gives a concrete example of contextual interpretation of numbers. Read it with Frigaliment and Nanakuli to separate proof of a usage, the parties’ connection to it, and its consistency with express language.

topics.assent: A shared commercial understanding can determine what the parties assented to even when a numerical phrase looks clear to outsiders.
topics.interpretation: The meaning of the protein specification depends on whether the alleged rounding practice formed part of the parties’ usage.
topics.trade-usage: The seller must be allowed to prove the trade practice and its relevance to the parties.

mnemonic.rationale: Horse meat scraps under fifty percent protein
